d.t: (colloquial) Used to imply connection between the speaker's experiences or activities and a group of listeners.
d.e: Hey guys, in this video I'll show you how I make my upside-down sponge cake. First, let's get our ingredients weighed out.

d.t: (Northern England, Scotland) Used before a person's name to indicate that the person is in one's family, or is a very close friend.
d.e: I'm going to see our Terry for tea.

d.t: Misspelling of are.
d.e: You our the lifeblood of the game and we thank you for everything you do. https://www.basketballengland.co.uk/news/2022/2022-basketball-england-awards-national-winners-announced/

d.t: Away from the inside or centre.
d.e: The magician tapped the hat, and a rabbit jumped out.

d.t: Away from, or at a distance from, some point of reference or focus.
d.e: Once they had landed, the commandos quickly spread out along the beach.

d.t: (informal) Away, or at a distance, in time (relative to, and usually before, a stated event, or into the future) (often preceded by a stated time period and followed by "from" or "to")
d.e: Five weeks out from the passage of the law, something has to change.

d.t: Outside; not indoors.
d.e: Last night we slept out under the stars.

d.t: (sports) Of the ball or other playing implement, so as to pass or be situated beyond the bounds of the playing area.
d.e: The football caught the edge of the line but then bounced out.

d.t: Into a state of non-operation or non-existence.
d.e: Turn the lights out.

d.t: To the end; completely; so that nothing remains.
d.e: I haven’t finished. Hear me out.

d.t: Used to intensify or emphasize.
d.e: The place was all decked out for the holidays.

d.t: Into a state of existence or visibility.
d.e: The singer is bringing out a new album next month.

d.t: (cricket, baseball, of a player) So as to be disqualified from playing further by some action of a member of the opposing team (such as being stumped in cricket or a forced out in baseball).
d.e: Wilson was bowled out for five runs.

d.t: (informal, sometimes proscribed) From the inside to the outside of; out of.
d.e: throw it out the window; get it out your mind

d.t: A means of exit, escape, reprieve, etc.
d.e: They wrote the law to give those organizations an out.

d.t: (baseball) A state in which a member of the batting team is removed from play due to the application of various rules of the game such as striking out, hitting a fly ball which is caught by the fielding team before bouncing, etc.

(cricket) A dismissal; a state in which a member of the batting team finishes his turn at bat, due to the application of various rules of the game, such as the bowler knocking over the batsman's wicket with the ball.
(poker) A card which can make a hand a winner.
(dated) A trip out; an outing.
(chiefly in the plural) One who, or that which, is out; especially, one who is out of office.
A place or space outside of something; a nook or corner; an angle projecting outward; an open space.
(printing, dated) A word or words omitted by the compositor in setting up copy; an omission.
(film, colloquial) An outtake.
(obsolete) A dram glass.
(transitive) To eject; to expel.
(intransitive) To come or go out; to get out or away; to become public, revealed, or apparent.
(transitive) To reveal (a person or organization) as having a certain secret, such as a being a secret agent or undercover detective.
d.e: 2009 March 16, Maurna Desmond, "AIG Outs Counterparties" (online news article), Forbes.com.

d.t: (transitive) To reveal (a secret).
d.e: A Brazilian company outed the new mobile phone design.

d.t: (transitive, LGBTQ) To reveal (a person) as LGBTQ+ (gay, trans, etc.).
To kill; to snuff out.
Not inside or within a place, especially a place that someone or something was formerly inside or is customarily inside:
d.e: I worked away cleaning the U-bend until all the gunge was out.

d.t: Not (or no longer) acceptable or in consideration, play, availability, or operation:
Open or public (about something).
Freed from secrecy.
d.e: My secret is out.

d.t: Available to be seen, or to be interacted with in some way:
(of the tide) At or near its lowest level.
d.e: You can walk to the island when the tide's out.

d.t: Without; no longer in possession of; not having any more.
d.e: Do you have any bread? Sorry, we're out.

d.t: (UK, Australia, of calculations or measurements) Containing errors or discrepancies, or in error by a stated amount.
d.e: Nothing adds up in this report. All these figures are out.

d.t: (procedure word, especially military) A radio procedure word meaning that the station is finished with its transmission and does not expect a response.
d.e: Destruction. Two T-72s destroyed. Three foot mobiles down. Out.

d.t: Get out; begone; away!
The part of something that faces out; the outer surface.
d.e: He's repainting the outside of his house.

d.t: The external appearance of someone or something.
d.e: Her outside was stern, but inside was a heart of gold.

d.t: The space beyond some limit or boundary.
d.e: Viewed from the outside, the building seemed unremarkable.

d.t: The furthest limit, as to number, quantity, extent, etc.
d.e: It may last a week at the outside.

d.t: The part of a road towards the central division: towards the right if one drives on the left, or towards the left if one drives on the right.
d.e: On a motorway, you should always overtake other vehicles on the outside.

d.t: The side of a curved road, racetrack etc. that has the longer arc length; the side of a racetrack furthest from the interior of the course or some other point of reference.
d.e: On the final bend, the second-place car tried to go around the outside of the leader but spun off into the barrier.

d.t: (surfing) The outer part of the sea, away from the peak of a wave.
(dated, UK, colloquial) A passenger riding on the outside of a coach or carriage.
Of or pertaining to the outer surface, limit or boundary.
d.e: The outside surface looks good.

d.t: Of, pertaining to or originating from beyond the outer surface, limit or boundary.
d.e:
1938 (believed written c.1933), H. P. Lovecraft, The Book,
Dogs had a fear of me, for they felt the outside shadow which never left my side.

d.t: Away from the interior or center of something.
Originating from, arranged by, or being someone outside an organization, group, etc.
d.e: The Board did not trust outside information about their rivals.

d.t: Extending or going beyond the borders or scope of an organization, group, etc.
(baseball, of a pitch) Away (far) from the batter as it crosses home plate.
d.e: The first pitch is ... just a bit outside.

d.t: Reaching the extreme or farthest limit, as to extent, quantity, etc; maximum.
d.e: an outside estimate

d.t: (chiefly UK) Positioned towards the central division of a road: towards the right-hand side if one drives on the left, or left-hand side if one drives on the right.
d.e: the outside lane of the motorway

d.t: (chiefly US) Positioned towards the shoulder of a road: towards the left-hand side if one drives on the left, or right-hand side if one drives on the right.
d.e: the outside lane of the highway

d.t: (of a person) Not legally married to or related to (e.g. not born in wedlock to), and/or not residing with, a specified other person (parent, child, or partner); (of a marriage, relationship, etc) existing between two such people. (Compare out of wedlock, nonresidential.)
d.e: The legitimacy and inheritance rights of children were questionable, because colonial law did not acknowledge the validity of an outside marriage contracted after a monogamous, Christian one.

d.t: To or in the outdoors or outside; to or in an area that is beyond the scope, limits, or borders of a given place.
d.e: I am going outside.

d.t: Outdoors.
d.e: I slept outside last night.

d.t: On the outside of, not inside (something, such as a building).
d.e:
1919 June 28, the Allied and Associated Powers and Germany, Treaty of Versailles, Part IV—German Rights and Interests outside Germany,
In territory outside her European frontiers as fixed by the present Treaty, Germany renounces all rights, titles and privileges whatever in or over territory which belonged to her or to her allies, and all rights, titles and privileges whatever their origin which she held as against the Allied and Associated Powers.

d.t: Beyond the scope, limits, or borders of.
d.e: tourists from outside the country

d.t: Near, but not in.
d.e: Jane Green […] lives outside New York City with her husband and children.

d.t: (usually with “of”) Except, apart from.
d.e: Outside of winning the lottery, the only way to succeed is through many years of hard work.

d.t: (transitive) To ostracize or exclude.
Finished; ended; concluded.
d.e: The show isn't over until the fat lady sings.

d.t: (informal, of an ongoing situation) Hopeless; irrecoverable.
d.e: We're keeping our marriage going for the sake of the kids, but really it's over.

d.t: (informal) Visiting one's home or other location.
d.e: My sister's over for the week.

d.t: Having surmounted an obstacle.
d.e: The horse struggled at that fence, but it's over.

d.t: (informal) Having an excess in a particular respect.
d.e: This steak is well over. (overcooked)

d.t: Surplus to requirements.
d.e: I made 20 cakes, but I only need 18, so there are two over.

d.t: (professional wrestling slang) Of a wrestler: generating a reaction from fans.
Describing a physical change of position or state.
Expressing figurative movement from one position or state across to another.
d.e: He came over to our way of thinking on the new project.

d.t: Indicating a direction or location away from the speaker, usually roughly horizontally or visualised as such.
d.e: I'll see you over at the club.

d.t: Thoroughly; completely; from beginning to end.
d.e: Let's talk over the project at tomorrow's meeting.

d.t: (often in compounds) To a high or excessive degree; overly; see also over-.
d.e: I'm not over bothered about going to the party.

d.t: Beyond or in excess of what is correct or expected.
d.e: The show ran ten minutes over.

d.t: To a future time.
d.e: Carry the shortfall over and we'll make it up tomorrow.

d.t: Overnight (throughout the night).
d.e: We missed the last bus home so we stayed over.

d.t: Indicating repetition.
See also individual entries for phrasal verbs: go over, hand over, run over, take over, win over, etc.
(cricket) A set of six legal balls bowled.
d.e: Jones hit four boundaries in the first over.

d.t: Any surplus amount of money, goods delivered, etc.
(informal) Something having an excess of a particular property.
d.e: I went fishing but caught mostly overs.

d.t: (gambling) A bet that a particular sporting statistic, such as points scored in a game, will be above a certain stated value.
(rare, dialectal or obsolete) A shore, riverbank.
Expressing spatial relationship or movement.
Expressing comparison.
During or throughout (a time period).
d.e: He's got grumpier over the years.

d.t: Through or via (a particular transmission medium).
d.e: A stern voice boomed over the loudspeaker.

d.t: Indicating relative status, authority, or power.
d.e: The owner's son lorded it over the experienced managers.

d.t: In a position of having overcome (a problem or issue); past; finished with; from one state to another via a hindrance that must be solved or defeated; or via a third state that represents a significant difference from the first two.
d.e: We got over the engineering problems and the prototype works great.

d.t: While doing an activity involving (something), especially while consuming.
d.e: We had a chat over dinner.

d.t: Concerning or regarding.
d.e: The two boys had a fight over whose girlfriend was the best.

d.t: Above, implying superiority after a contest; in spite of; notwithstanding.
d.e: We triumphed over difficulties.

d.t: Expressing causation: due to, as the result of.
d.e: He was fired over that.

d.t: (mathematics) Divided by.
d.e: Two over six equals one over three.

d.t: (poker) Separates the three of a kind from the pair in a full house.
d.e: 9♦9♠9♣6♥6♠ = nines over sixes

d.t: (procedure word, military) A radio procedure word meaning that the station is finished with its transmission and is expecting a response.
d.e: Bravo Six, this is Bravo Six Four. Stand by for ten mike report one dash three, over.

d.t: Instructs the reader to turn the page and continue reading the other side.
(obsolete, slang) Ellipsis of over the left shoulder (“expressing disbelief etc.”).
(UK, transitive, dialect, obsolete) To go over, or jump over.
d.e: He overed the fence in good style.

d.t: (UK, intransitive, dialect, obsolete) To run about.
d.e: The cattle have been overing all day because of the flies.

d.t: Belonging to; possessed; acquired and designated by; proper to; property of; titled to; held in one's name; under/using the name of. Often marks a possessive determiner as reflexive, referring back to the subject of the clause or sentence.
Not shared.
d.e: When we move into the new house, the kids will each have their own bedroom.

d.t: (obsolete) Peculiar, domestic.
(obsolete) Not foreign.
(transitive) To have rightful possession of (property, goods or capital); to have legal title to; to acquire a property or asset.
d.e: I own this car.

d.t: (transitive) To have recognized political sovereignty over a place, territory, as distinct from the ordinary connotation of property ownership.
d.e: The United States owns Point Roberts by the terms of the Treaty of Oregon.

d.t: (transitive, informal) To defeat or embarrass; to overwhelm.
d.e: I will own my enemies.

d.t: (transitive) To virtually or figuratively enslave.
(online gaming, slang) To defeat, dominate, or be above.
(transitive, computing, slang) To illicitly obtain administrative access to a computer system, thereby having full access to all the files thereon (including executables).
(intransitive, slang) To be very good.
(intransitive) To admit, concede, grant, allow; not to deny.
(transitive) To acknowledge.
d.e: I must own that I have been at fault all this time.

d.t: (transitive) To proudly acknowledge; to not be ashamed or embarrassed of.
(transitive) To take responsibility for.
(transitive) To recognise.
d.e: I own him as a son of my own.

d.t: (Internet slang) A crushing insult.
